captions.text: This is fevm-replay.
It runs real Ethereum mainnet transactions inside fevm, the EVM written in Fe,
and checks that each one ends exactly as it did on chain.
115,213 mainnet transactions, and no fevm bug:
every difference was traced to a cause outside the interpreter.
Now the headline:
every root in the header comes out of fevm.
The parent's Merkle proofs are a witness:
fevm runs the block on it,
writes its end state into that partial trie and hashes it again.
That must be the header's state root, as a stateless client checks it.
Every other root must match too.
Here is that run:
block 26,424,805, checked by CI on every push.
71 of 71 transactions match.
They re-encode to the transactions root, the requests hash matches,
and the state root is the header's.
It also estimates EIP-7864's binary-tree witness:
about half (stems and values exact, depth and positions assumed),
505 to 557 KiB against 1,002.
Change one withdrawal by one wei, and the withdrawals root,
the end-state proof and the computed state root all fail.
A clean run rests on one 32-byte block hash.
Fe functions declare their effects.
The function that decides match or diff gets a text buffer and nothing else,
so calling the network from it is a type error.
Is a Fe port a drop-in replacement?
Ask mainnet.
The USDT port ran in 21,230 mainnet transactions, and none behaved differently.
DAI's certificate:
10,562 mainnet transactions, 211,240 mutated runs, none different,
all 21 planted mutants caught.
The explorer shows where two runs part:
before its fix, the Fe port reverted on a bot's packed address.
After the fix, they no longer part.
Opcode by opcode, Fe spends 44% less gas than solc on stack shuffling,
but 25% more on memory.
No Fe install needed:
the release binary runs the seven saved mainnet fixtures, and all seven match.
fevm-replay validates whole mainnet blocks statelessly,
measures what stateless Ethereum would cost,
and runs Ethereum's own system contracts in Fe.
It found three bugs in the Fe ports, two node tracer bugs,
and what the Osaka fork changed.
Code on GitHub, results at fevm-replay.vercel.app.
Three consecutive mainnet blocks, in one run.
Block one:
230 transactions, all matching.
Block two:
Block three:
And the links hold:
each block's parent is the one before it,
its pre-state proven against the state root fevm computed.
A follower takes the block two behind the chain head, proves it and validates it.
This page lists every block it took, with the witness per transaction and per million gas.
It also shows whose storage weighs the most:
the deeper a contract's storage trie, the more each slot it touches costs.
And what would stateless Ethereum cost?
Priced by the EIP-4762 draft, these same blocks would need 23% more gas.
35% of the transactions, sent with the gas limit they had, would run out of gas.
Exempt the block's coinbase, and it is 13%.
Fe can stand in for Ethereum's own code too.
Every block starts with two system calls, to contracts written in assembly.
Their Fe ports store what the header implies,
and answer all 16 reads as the deployed ones do:
on 51 mainnet blocks.
Mainnet transactions that read beacon roots run identically on the port.
